dev_notes: src/render/ledger-html.mjs builds the document, src/render/pdf.mjs drives Chromium via playwright-core (channel chrome, msedge, chromium, or $LEDGER_CHROME). editionFile() and printEdition() in src/commands/build.mjs decide where a file goes: a released version goes to output.client_dir under pdf_name, the future one to output.dir with -draft appended; `ledger cut` and `ledger build` share them. `ledger build [v3|all|draft]` picks editions (`--version N` still works), `--html` writes the page instead of printing it. Contents entries are plain <a href="#id"> anchors onto ids on the area heads (area-N) and the closing sections (closing-*); Chromium turns those into named destinations in the PDF. Fonts are static instances, not variable ones, or Chromium emits Type 3 glyphs that copy out shredded; after rendering, pdf.mjs asks Chromium (CSS.getPlatformFontsForNode) which font drew each element's text and fails the build if any is a system font; Noto Sans Symbols 2 is embedded last in both stacks for quoted UI icons. Before printing, releaseOversizedBlocks() in pdf.mjs lays the page out at Letter size and lifts break-inside: avoid from any block taller than a page, because Chromium otherwise pushes such a block to a fresh page and splits it there anyway, leaving a heading alone on an empty page; .cat-head, .sub-head and .feature .name keep break-after: avoid so a heading still travels with the first lines below it. The printed number comes from ReleaseSet.labelOf, which carries the nearest earlier display_version forward; it reaches the cover, footer, colophon, title, redraft note and pdf_name, and nothing else.

history.name: The printed edition for the client
history.description: The command ledger build prints a PDF of one release: a front page carrying the masthead, the feature count, a bar breaking those features down by size, and a note of what changed since the last edition, then every entry in reading order. The document is real HTML and CSS, printed through the Chrome or Edge already on the machine, with the two fonts embedded so text copies cleanly out of the finished file. Any edition can be reprinted at any time, and it reproduces exactly what was presented that day.

Each edition is a PDF: a front page carrying the masthead, the feature count, a bar breaking those features down by size, and a note of what changed since the last edition, then a contents list that links into the document, then every entry in reading order. ledger cut prints it into the client folder; ledger preview prints the open release as a draft, named with -draft and kept in the gitignored docs folder, so a draft is never mistaken for an edition. ledger build prints every cut edition that isn't on disk yet, and ledger build v3 reprints one with its entries as they stood that day, in their current wording. The fonts are embedded, so text copies cleanly out of the finished file, and display_version on a release in releases.json sets the number its edition prints.

Each edition is a PDF: a first page with the counts and what's new and what changed, then each change in full with how to see it, then one line for every feature. Each feature has one number throughout, and the PDF has bookmarks. ledger cut prints an edition; ledger preview prints a draft.
history.how_to_see: Run ledger preview and open the PDF. The numbers after each item on the first page lead to the entries that print the same number in their margin.

events.what: The front page led straight into the contents list, so the changes were only visible as stripes spread through the whole document. A summary page now sits between the two; see “Summary of changes”.

ledger preview takes --run, which hands an out-of-date summary to a coding agent before printing, and nothing else: a preview is for checking the release day to day, and an audit or a review costs a read of the code or of the whole release. See “Summary of changes”.
ledger preview opens with the size of the release and what moved since the last look, and a draft prints the recorded changes, marked as such, until they are composed.
events.why: A preview is how the size of the latest changes gets checked, and that shouldn't need a PDF or an agent. A draft with no notes at all hid the very changes it was printed to show.

events.what: An edition prints every new, updated and removed entry in full, with how to see it, and one line for each entry that didn't move, and the cover shows one line of counts instead of the size bar. ledger preview no longer has an agent compose first: where nothing is prepared, it shows the changes as recorded.
events.why: Reprinting every unchanged entry in full was most of an edition's length: this ledger's own second edition ran to 13 pages for 25 features. A preview is the free look at the release, and tokens are spent only when someone asks for them.

events.what: Every feature now carries one number, such as 2.4, which the first page, the changes in detail and the full list all cite, and the PDF has bookmarks for every part, area and changed entry.
events.why: A client should see at once what changed and what the product does, and find their way around the document without effort.
